editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Jasper E. Brady
sp.p: Birthdate and so forth right now.

sp.speaker: Carolyn Dominiak
sp.p: Um, yeah.

sp.speaker: Jasper E. Brady
sp.p: My name is Jasper E. Brady. My birthdate is November 2nd, 1924. I joined the Service in 1942. That is, I joined the Enlisted Reserve in 1942 when I was going to Culver Military Academy in Indiana. The reason I enlisted, which was with the Enlisted Reserve at the time, was the fact that if I hadn't enlisted in the Enlisted Reserve, I might have of been drafted before my third year of high school was finished. So, I went in the Enlisted Reserve. And part of the curriculum at the Military Academy I was going to was an R.O.T.C. training program for the-- in subjects that you would get in basic training in the Army.

So, I continued there at Culver Military Academy until I left in June of 1943, at which time I received orders to go to active duty in service, and I took my basic training at {coughs} -- sorry-- at-- in Georgia at-- can't think of the name of it. Just can't now. It was in the southern part of Georgia. And the basic training was 17 weeks long, and I took-- they gave us instruction in basic infantry subjects.

The unit that I was with was called heavy weapons basic, which meant that we took training in the .30 caliber machine gun, both the air-cooled and the water-cooled model. And also in the 81-millimeter mortar, which was the one that they used at that time. So, we took training in close-order drill, military map reading, that type of thing, first aid, School of the Soldier Without Arms, which was close-order drill. And we finished up our basic in December of 1943, and at which time, because of the fact that I was slated to go to Officer Candidates School because of my R.O.T.C. training at Culver, they sent me to a-- a unit in Columbus, Ohio to await assignment to Officer Candidates School. And I was there for a while. And it was pretty much a-- you might call it a country club atmosphere.

It -- we didn't have an awful lot of duties. We did-- we did things like working at the-- at the university. And pretty much, we were -- as I say, we were waiting for reassignment. We then, myself and three other soldiers who had gone to Culver, went to the University of Western Kentucky in Bowling Green, and we were part of the Army Specialized Training Program at that time, and of course is at the college. We were at the college for-- from the winter of 1943, `44 until the summer of 1944, at which time we were assigned to Officer Candidates School at the Armored School in Fort Knox, Kentucky.

The two gentlemen that I was with graduated from the Officer Candidates School. I did not. I was washed out for whatever reasons they-- they had. I was never told, but while we were at the Officer Candidates School we took training in armored force tanks and vehicles of that type; half-tracks, which are a vehicle that has tracks on the back and wheels on the front and usually carried sometimes only as .50 caliber machine gun and could transport troops, or some of them had 105-millimeter cannon mounted on the back, and they were used as a sort of a mechanized artillery. We took training in all types of vehicles.

We drove everything, most every vehicle that the Army had at the time, and took training in the M4 tank, which was-- which was the basic tank for the Army at that time. It was a-- what they called a medium tank. It had a 75-millimeter cannon on it, and also a .30 caliber machine gun mounted in the-- in the front of it, so that-- and a .30 caliber machine gun mounted next to the main gun so that they could cover the ground in front of them. Let's see. And also the-- the light tank which had a 37-millimeter cannon on it, and that was used-- that was one of the tanks that they used a lot in the Pacific because it was good for jungle warfare. It was a little more adaptable to close-in warfare like that, for that reason. And it -- not only did it fire a cannon shell, but it also fired a shell that was called canister, which had steel balls in the-- in the projectile so that when it went off it spread out, and that was good for close-in fire as in jungles or that type of thing.

So, when I left the Officer Candidates School at Fort Knox, I was assigned to Camp Shelby, Mississippi. And that was where the 65th Infantry Division was being formed up to go to Europe and join the people under General Eisenhower in that-- in that area. We-- when the division got completely formed, we went by train to a camp in New York State, whose name I cannot remember, and we went-- we were there getting all our shots for the European Theater and getting the equipment that we would need overseas and that sort of thing. And we went from there to the Port of Embarkation in New York City, and on a ship called the John Ericsson, which was a converted passenger liner, and that was-- that was in January of 1945. And we put our whole division, 15,000 men, on that one ship. And then we crossed the Atlantic and were slated to land in England and then take L.S.T.'s to France, but they got orders when we were halfway across that the Port of Le Havre was cleared and we could land in France instead of going to England.

So, our ship went-- was one of the first ones-- as a matter of fact, the first one to go in the Port of Le Havre, France and land troops there. So, we were -- landed at the port and went from the large ship that we were on to a smaller-- not L.S.T.'s, but I think L.C.I.'s is what they were called at that time, Landing Craft Infantry, and they took us into the-- into the port. And then we got on the trucks, and they took us to the camp that we were supposed to set up prior to our going into combat.

So, we were taken to a field just out of-- outside of the town of Saint Valerie (ph) and we were-- because of the fact that we were the first ones in that area, we had to set up the camp completely, put up what they call pyramidal tents which would hold approximately 20 men each. And they had to set up the tents and then construct company-- company streets out of crushed stone and whatever, and dig outdoor latrines.

And so we stayed there in that camp from January of `45 until we were inspected by General Patton with the idea of-- of our going to join his Third Army in the southern part of France. That inspection was completed, and we were sent into combat in-- at the end of March, 1945. Now, I guess I forgot to tell you that I was in a cannon company, which was a company that used 105 Howitzers in support of infantry troops. And so we set up our guns just outside of a city by the name of Saarlautern. We were slated to acquire support for the 260th Infantry Regiment, which is the regiment that we were attached to, and we fired from there on any targets that -- {coughs}. I don't suppose I could get a glass of water.

sp.speaker: Carolyn Dominiak
sp.p: Absolutely. I'll -- Stop this for a minute.
[tape stopped]

sp.speaker: Jasper E. Brady
sp.p: As I was saying, I belonged to the cannon company which had 105-- 105-millimeter Howitzers, four of them. When we got to the town of Saarlautern we set up our guns and were given targets of opportunity to-- in support of the infantry who was in Saarlautern, and the Germans were at the other side of the city, and we were trying to push them out of there, and so we fired at whatever target we were given. There was one method of fire that was particularly impressive, and that was what they called time on target, where they had the 81-millimeter mortars, the 105 Howitzers in our company, the 105 Howitzers in the artillery, and the 105 Howitzers -- 155 Howitzers, 155-millimeter, all tied in together, so that when they gave a command to fire, the ones that were closest-- or let's see. No. The ones that were farthest away fired first, and then going down the line each battery fired getting closer to the enemy, and the last ones to fire were the 81-millimeter mortars so that they had a time so that all this fire fell on the enemy at the same time.

So you had 81-millimeter mortar shells, 105-millimeter Howitzers, large and small, and 155-millimeter Howitzers all blowing on the same target. And I would not like to be there when that happened. And while we were there, the German army who at that time was pretty much decimated, although they still had some-- some air power, their ground forces were still fighting. They sent a reconnaissance plane over our position, and he was high enough up so that our anti-aircraft or artillery couldn't touch him, but he took pictures from his aircraft of our position and plotted them on a map, and then took them back to the German 88-millimeter batteries, and they fired at us in-- with just map coordinates. They came within 25 yards of our position, which is pretty darn good when you think about it. But the German-- the German 88's were a very accurate weapon, and, you know, a projectile. 88 millimeters in diameter, which would be -- 75 was three inches, 88 millimeter would be between three and four inches in diameter. And it was a small projectile, maybe 10 inches to a foot long, and it had a very long shell with a lot of powder in it which gave it a very high velocity when it was fired, and very-- made it very accurate also.

So, that was what they were shooting at us with. They had another-- had a method of lighting up the battle field at night when there was-- when there was cloud cover over the battle field. They would shine search lights up at the clouds so that the reflection from the clouds would give you a-- which would light up the battle field almost as if it was daytime, or maybe not quite that bright, but say under a full moon. So that we were able to work in the dark because they lit it up for us. When we left there, we went across Germany. We were right on the border between France and Germany when we initially went into action. And we went-- we went across Germany up to the northern part of Germany to a city called Hersfeld. And we were there in April -- first part of April in 1945, which was just before Easter. Then we started south towards Austria, and on our way there we were in the vicinity of a German concentration camp called Ohrdruf, and that's where the Germans had imprisoned some of the Jewish prisoners that they took and were part of the Holocaust. And we were-- General Patton, who was our army commander, decided that all the troops should go through this camp and see just exactly what the atrocities were that they were using against the Jews, and so we saw things like bodies stacked up like cord wood or thrown into open pits and covered with lime, and then covered over with dirt so that the bodies would decompose. And it was a pretty frightening thing to see. And, of course, some of the-- some of the prisoners who were still there, and they were pretty much down to skin and bones, and some of them were so weak they couldn't walk and had to be taken out in stretchers. This was similar to camps like Bergen-Belsen and some of the other camps in Northeastern Germany, and they were all very similar. They had the-- they had the ovens where they burned the corpses when they died, and it was a pretty gruesome sight. And if anybody should tell you that the Holocaust didn't happen, it did. I saw it. And we went from there, that area -- while we were in that area, incidentally, that was around toward the middle of April 1945, on April 12th, 1945 President Roosevelt died, which was a shock to everybody. And we were on our way down to Austria at that time. We went through the City of Ravensburg in Austria, and then went from there down into Linz, Austria, which is on the Danube River. And while we were in Linz, the war ended, so we were doing occupation duty in the City of Linz. How's the tape coming? Okay?

sp.speaker: Carolyn Dominiak
sp.p: Good.

sp.speaker: Jasper E. Brady
sp.p: We were-- my gun section was stationed at the main police station in Linz, and we were there for a short time after the war ended, which was on May 7th, 1945. The war in Europe anyway. And then we were sent to a small town up on the border between Austria and Czechoslovakia to do occupation duty there and guard the border to keep an eye on people that were crossing the border between Austria and Czechoslovakia and find out who they were and why they were traveling and so forth. Most the people we just let through. We would, every once in a while, get German or Hungarian troops that were part of the German Army coming down through there, and we had to stop them and check them out. Of course, everybody had surrendered by that time, so some of them were -- were allowed to go back to their homes. And so we did occupation duty in this little town by the name of Putzleinsdorf, and it was a-- it was a farming town. And we were staying at a small inn in the center of the town and were able, on our off-duty times, to go out in the countryside and hunt deer with our army rifles, which was not too good a thing to do because the ammunition that we were using in our rifles was called armor piercing ammunition. If we shot it at a deer, it would go right in one side and out the other and he wouldn't even stop.

So -- but at any rate, we got some deer and had the people at this inn that we were staying at prepare them for-- for us, and that was-- that was kind of nice. And we were there in this little town until July of 1945, and then we got orders to go back to the States with the idea that we would be -- when we got to the States we'd get a 30-day furlough and be sent to the Pacific Theater. But it turned out that by the time we got back to the States, which was the first part of August of `45, the Japanese surrendered after they had dropped the atom bomb. And so we were reassigned-- we were given 30 days' leave, and then we were reassigned to outfits in the United States. I was sent to Camp Campbell, Kentucky, where I was part of the 11th Infantry Regiment, and which was assigned-- let's see-- in the-- in the autumn of 1945 to go to the island of Adak in the Aleutian Chain. And we were up there to test cold and wet weather equipment. The outfit that went up there consisting of our-- our regiment and some support troops was called Task Force Willawong (ph), and we were sent up to Adak to do testing of cold and wet weather equipment. And we had all sorts of exercises where we-- we camped out in the snow and tested different types of tents and different types of cold weather parkas and boots and that type of thing. I was there with that group until December of 1945, and then I was-- my enlistment period was up at that time, and I was sent back to the States on a ship. And on the way back through the Bering Sea, which was in the area where the Aleutian Islands are, went from Adak down towards the Western United States, we were due to dock at San Francisco, but we ran into a storm. And the waves were -- some of the waves that we saw were 30, 40 feet high. And it stove in the bow of our ship, and because of the fact that the ship was in such bad shape, instead of going to San Francisco, we went to Fort Lewis, Washington, just outside of Seattle. We docked in Seattle and then went to Fort Lewis. And I was-- I was, along with some others, sent by train to Fort Devens, Massachusetts where I was separated from the Service because my enlistment was up. And I spent about a year and a half as a civilian doing various things. Took training as a store manager for F.W. Woolworth. That didn't work out so well.
So I went to work for a company called World Book Encyclopedia and sold encyclopedias for a while. Didn't like that very much, and decided to go back into the Service again.

So, in -- in September of 1948 I enlisted in the Service and was sent to Fort Devens, Massachusetts and then to Fort Dix, New Jersey where I took some refresher courses because I'd been out for a while. And myself and some others were sent to Fort Knox, Kentucky as-- to train newly enlisted men in army basic. And that was an eight weeks course, and I lived outside the post in a house trailer, and went into work at usually about 7:00 o'clock in the morning and did the reveille formation, and then we went out to train troops. And it was pretty much like-- almost like a civilian job. We went in at 7:00 in the morning and were finished at 5:00 at night, and we could go back home to our-- to our wives.
So, that was kind of nice duty, but that ended very abruptly when we were sent to a Second Infantry Division in Fort Lewis, Washington. From there I went to Korea. What do you want to do now?

sp.speaker: Carolyn Dominiak
sp.p: We can go straight into Korea if you'd like. Just whatever feels natural for you.

sp.speaker: Jasper E. Brady
sp.p: Okay. Fine. We-- I was-- as I say, I was sent to Fort Lewis, Washington to the Second Infantry Division, and we were formed up as a-- as an infantry division, and I was in what they called a heavy weapons company. And I was a-- assigned as a machine gunner for heavy water-cooled machine gun, .30 caliber. And we were-- when we got all of our equipment and we had to get a special inoculation for different types of things that we might pick up in the Pacific, like cholera and malaria and that sort of thing, and so we got those shots. And then the division was-- was fully formed, so then we got on -- on a ship and were sent to Korea. We landed in Pusan, Korea. And at that time the American forces had been pushed back so that they were on a very narrow perimeter around the City of Pusan, so we-- our division, along with the First Marine Division, which came over about the same time that we did, were put into-- into line in this perimeter and started fighting our way up the Korean Peninsula, pushing the North Koreans back, slowly but surely.

That-- while we were about halfway up the peninsula, General MacArthur was in command of some troops who landed in Incheon, which was the seaport for the City of Seoul in Korea. And they came in at the northern end of South Korea, and came in behind the lines of the North Koreans and effectively cut them off, but they were able to retreat back across the 38th Parallel and regroup. And so then we went across the 38th Parallel for the first time and up into what is now called North Korea. And some of the encounters we had were-- I-- I myself had some very close calls at several different times. One time we were-- we had gone into position during the day and stayed in-- I had dug a foxhole, which was about six feet deep which I could get down into in case of enemy fire. And we had a enemy mortar out in front of us behind a hill that it was close enough so that we could hear the shells leave the-- go off in the tube of the mortar and come towards us. And as soon as that-- that occurred, why, we would get back into our-- get down into our holes. And this one time I was sitting up on the top of my foxhole eating a can of sea rations, and we heard the mortar shells coming in, so I got down into my hole and put the can of sea rations on the edge of the hole. After the mortar barrage was over, I got up, and the can of sea rations, which was right on the edge of my hole, was completely filled with holes from the shrapnel from the mortar rounds, so that if my head had been above that hole, it would have been torn off by shrapnel.

So, that was one of the close calls that I had. And then immediately after that-- that night we were supposed to pull back to a-- an auxiliary position further to the rear from our position, and for some reason or other the group that I was with got-- got cut off from the rest of the company, and we-- when the sun came up in the morning, we found ourselves on the top of a hill all by ourselves. There was about-- oh, I would say maybe not more than two dozen of us there. We had a-- we had a couple machine guns and there were rifle troops. And we found that the North Koreans were-- we were on one side of the hill and the North Koreans were down on the other side, and they were throwing hand grenades over the top of the hill and rolling them down the other side towards us. And while this was going on, the-- at one point they threw a grenade over the hill, and it rolled down and it landed right beside me. And the only thing I could think to do, and it happened on the split second, was to fall down flat on the ground.

And luckily it was the right thing to do because the hand grenade burst and went over the top of me and just knocked a piece of-- knocked a part of my field pack, made a hole in it, but didn't hurt me at all. That was close call number two. And then when-- while we were there, we knew we were cut off and weren't sure whether anybody was coming to relieve us or not, and we didn't know exactly what to do, so we talked it over and decided, well, there were some that said that they felt that they ought to stay right there and not-- not leave, and there were some that said that-- might have me being one of them -- thought that we should try and get away from there and get back in touch with our main unit. Well, there was about half of the men that decided to do that, so we went down to the bottom of the hill and got together and -- [Interruption by unidentified person]. VOICE: Oh, excuse me. I didn't see you in here.

sp.speaker: Jasper E. Brady
sp.p: We got together. We had one machine gun and several riflemen, and we went down an area between two hills. There were North Koreans up on the top of one hill firing down at us and one of the fellows that was with us got wounded and the -- the others helped him out. And we went down this draw between two hills and found the road that went south. And so, just as we started to go down that road, we looked behind us and saw North Korean troops coming up the road towards us.

Somebody said, "Well, we don't know whether those-- those are our troops or not." And then they started shooting at us, and so I said to him, "Does that answer your questions?" We started up the road and we were running as fast as we could towards a position where we saw that our troops were, and got there ahead of them and rejoined our outfit and went-- withdrew further back from there. So, found out later that the fellows that stayed there, for whatever reason they thought was necessary, were-- most of them were taken prisoner, but some of them were killed by the North Koreans.
So, that told us that we had made the right decision to get out of there. And we-- once we got back and reorganized, we went-- came up that same road again and took those same positions back--
[END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE ONE; BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE]

-- way up north in Korea to the City of Pyongyang to start out, which is the capital of North Korea. And we went through that city and up to the Yalu River, which was the border between North Korea and China. We reached that area about Thanksgiving of 1951. Yeah. Now, wait a minute. No. It was Thanksgiving of 1950. At that time we had our -- we had our Thanksgiving dinner up there. We were-- turkey and all the fixings we brought up into the field, and we had a very nice Thanksgiving dinner. And that night the Chinese broke through our lines north of us, and we were-- started to be pushed back towards the 38th Parallel again.

Sort of an amusing occurrence happened at that particular place. The Chinese were up on the hills around us firing down at us, and everybody was looking for a foxhole to get into, protect themselves from the incoming fire. And I found -- I found a foxhole I thought somebody had dug, put rocks around it and was sort of in a square shape, and I jumped in there. And while I was protected from the incoming fire, but the only problem was that it wasn't a foxhole that I jumped into. It was an old Korean latrine, and the stuff in the bottom of the hole was about a foot to inches deep, so it came up to -- almost to the top of my boots. And I had to wear those boots until-- for the next three months, which was not very pleasant. {Laughing}.

sp.speaker: Carolyn Dominiak
sp.p: {Laughing}.

sp.speaker: Jasper E. Brady
sp.p: And then we slowly withdrew from that area back towards the 38th Parallel. The Chinese, of course, along with their North Korean allies pushed us back because the Chinese were-- had many more troops than we did, and so we were pushed back slowly and fought several delaying actions. And in one area that we were in -- I was at that time was attached to the headquarters company, or the headquarters platoon of our company, and we were able to pitch our pup tents. I should probably say that a pup tent is a tent which is about six feet long and maybe three feet high on the inside, and it's usually two-- two pieces of canvas buttoned together, which-- and occupied by two men.

So, we were able to pitch these tents and sleep in them at night. And one night we were-- we were attacked by the Chinese just before dawn, and we had to get out and protect ourselves the best way we could. And we were retreating back, and I got separated from-- from the group that I was with, and I was at the bottom of a hill, and I wasn't exactly sure where I was, so-- And as a sort of a side comment to this, when you're given your basic training and you're told that when you are on the top of a hill not to stand up, but to stay down so that you give a low profile to anybody that's observing you or has a bead on you with a rifle or machine gun or whatever.

So, I went to the top of this hill and did the thing that I was not supposed to do, was stand up and look around. And I heard a crack, which was the-- a rifle-- somebody had shot a rifle at me, and it went apparently close to my head, and I heard it go by. And I immediately threw myself down and went down below the hill again. Came back later to that same place with some of the other ones in our group, and we looked up on the hill above us, and there was a cave. And some of our troops had captured a sniper that was in that cave and had a bead right on the top of the hill that I was standing on, and he-- he shot at me. Luckily for me, he was a poor shot and missed me.

So, that was another one of the close calls that I had. And then we started withdrawing back from that area towards the 38th Parallel again, and the Chinese were close on our heels. Matter of fact, the Chinese were behind us at one time. Our division was completely surrounded, but we had to fight our way out. They were so far back that they were behind our division headquarters, which was several mile-- usually several miles back from the-- the main line.

So, we were-- we were pulling back, and we got into one position and were camped in a small town that was surrounded by rice fields. And the Chinese attacked us while we were in that position, and we were completely outnumbered, so we withdrew back through a road. And the road that we went down where the-- that was-- we were -- most of us were on -- either on the back of or in vehicles going down this road. And the particular vehicle I was with, it was a-- it was an army jeep, and it had a -- room on the back of it to stand on, and I was standing on it and going down this road. And I looked to both sides of the road, and people were getting-- people were getting killed on both sides of the road, but for some reason or other, those of us that were on the road weren't getting shot at. Just the people in the fields on both sides. Never could figure that out. Then we went from there down to an area where we were reorganized again. And the group that I was with was-- I was with what was called a 75-millimeter recoilless rifle platoon, and we had-- had lost our vehicles, and our weapons-- our 75 recoilless rifle weapons, which was like a cannon.

And so we were in an area, and sort of a large field, and the company that I was with was told to leave this area and go up to a hill to defend the area where we were retreating from. And so we started up that hill, and one of the fellows was injured on the way up to the hill, sprained or broke his ankle, and I was told to help him back to the aid station, and I did. And by the time I got to the aid station and -- it was almost dark, so I wasn't able to rejoin the troops that I was with, so I stayed with this other outfit. And we were put in trucks and sent back to the rear. And on the-- on the way back we were fired on by the-- by the Chinese, and then we had to get out of the trucks and go through a field. And when we got to the other end of this field, we came across the Canadian Princess Pat Regiment, which was occupying a position then.

They had tanks, and they were -- they were there, and so we went back through them. And they were defending this particular area, and so we went back through them and started towards the rear. And while I was in the truck I was-- I got a wound in my right hand from the-- from the side-- the front side of the carbine that I was carrying. And so I went to an aid station to get that fixed up so that it wouldn't get infected or anything. And so they-- the British put a bandage on it, and I started down the-- down the road again, and some British troops came by in a truck and they saw the bandage on my hand and picked me up and took me back to the rear.

And I was able to, after I'd gone to the hospital and had my hand fixed up, then I was able to rejoin my company, and we went-- went back into action again. And we were assigned a hill, which was called Hill 1149, meaning that it was 1,149 meters high overlooking the main supply route. And we were to take-- take the hill from the Chinese and-- and then stay there and keep the hill to protect the main supply route down below us. And so we started. We went up that hill, and we got to one point in the hill, and the Chinese were out in front of us dug into bunkers made of logs and sandbags, and we couldn't get them out with mortars or artillery, so we -- we called in supporting fire from the 16-inch guns from the Battleship Missouri, which was out in the-- out in the sea on that side of the peninsula, which was the west side of the peninsula. And they gave us supporting fire with their 16-inch guns and fired on these bunkers. And they had artillery that had shells that penetrated the bunkers and then blew them up, so then we were able to go a little bit further. And my-- the company I was with was in reserve, and there were a couple of other companies out in front of us that were in the main part of the fight, and we were-- we were behind on the reverse slope of a hill, and the rest of the company was on the forward slope, and they were fighting their way to gain control of the hill.

So, I was sitting on-- on the side of the hill, and there was a lot of shrapnel flying around, and a piece of it came down and embedded itself into my right knee. It was a piece about as long as your index finger, about that thick, and I picked it out with my fingers, and it was naturally very hot, and I dropped it and then picked it up and -- when it cooled off and gave it to one of the fellows that was with me. I probably should have kept it for a souvenir, but I didn't. And then the medics came-- came over and put a bandage on my knee and sent me back to the battalion aid station, which was about a mile and a half back from our position. I went to that battalion aid station, and they checked over the wound to see that it wasn't bleeding profusely or anything, and they found it to be okay, so they put me on one of these helicopters with the bubbles on both sides to-- such as they used in the movie M.A.S.H., and sent me back to the M.A.S.H. hospital, which was behind the lines, and I was there. They cleaned out my wound and gave me a tetanus shot and then sent me back to Japan. And that's when I left Korea. I was-- I had been in Korea long enough that I had what they call rotation points, and I had enough points to go back to the States.

So, because of the fact that I was wounded, I was able to go back by plane, and landed in San Francisco, and then was sent back to Fort Devens, Massachusetts where I met my wife. And I was-- from Fort Devens I was sent to Camp Kilmer, New Jersey, and I was-- what I wanted to do was go to Fort Dix, New Jersey as-- train troops as I was doing before I left for Korea, but they decided that they wanted me in Camp Kilmer, New Jersey on the post (furnace) firing detail. Why they thought that, I don't know. But anyway, that's where I went. And then I was-- I decided to-- when my enlistment was up to take my discharge and leave the Service. So I left the Service in May of 1952. Do you want to stop here?

sp.speaker: Carolyn Dominiak
sp.p: I think we can actually go on to a couple questions about after your discharge, if that's all right.

sp.speaker: Jasper E. Brady
sp.p: All right. Okay.

sp.speaker: Carolyn Dominiak
sp.p: Let's see. What-- what did you go on to do as a career after the war?

sp.speaker: Jasper E. Brady
sp.p: Well, when I first got out, I-- of course, I went right from high school into the Service, so I wasn't really trained for anything in particular. So, the first job I held was-- was as a milkman, delivering milk. And that was pretty good, but it was pretty-- it was-- I just wasn't suited to the-- to it. It was-- it was a job which you had to-- demanded a lot of very fast work all during the day, and then-- and I just didn't adapt to it.

So, then I applied for a job with the Pratt Whitney Company in Connecticut, and they trained me to be a parts inspector. And I got a job with them in one of their plants in-- just outside of Meriden, Connecticut where I was living at that time. And I worked there, and then they transferred me to East Hartford -- oh, no. While I was there I went to electronics school on the G.I. Bill. I went there in the daytime. I quit my position at Pratt Whitney as an inspector at that time and went to electronics school on the G.I. Bill and became an electronics technician. And then I went back to-- back to work as a technician for Pratt Whitney for a while. And I went from working for Pratt Whitney to a couple of other places. And I was -- the electronics trade, being what it is, I was laid off at several companies. And because of the-- one went bankrupt and-- a couple went bankrupt on me, matter of fact. And I had to find a job someplace else, so-- but I was working as an electronics technician for about 25 years, different companies. I ended up here in Rochester working for Xerox, and that's where I was just before I retired. I was a contract technician for-- working for -- for Xerox and Kodak. And after a while, the-- the economy being what it was at that time, didn't have enough work for me, and so I decided to try something else. And so I went into real estate, and I sold real estate for about four years, and then I retired. So, that's where I am now.

sp.speaker: Carolyn Dominiak
sp.p: What -- what year did you retire in?

sp.speaker: Jasper E. Brady
sp.p: In 1984, I believe it was.

sp.speaker: Carolyn Dominiak
sp.p: Did you ever join a veterans organization?

sp.speaker: Jasper E. Brady
sp.p: I joined the American Legion for a while, but I found that it wasn't exactly the type of organization that I wanted to be in. The American Legion does a lot of good things, and I can't fault them for-- for anything they've done or haven't done, but it just didn't seem to be the type of organization that I wanted to be in.

sp.speaker: Carolyn Dominiak
sp.p: And, finally, how did your service both in Korea and in World War II affect your life after that point?

sp.speaker: Jasper E. Brady
sp.p: Well, the first year when I came back from Korea I didn't think that it had affected it-- affected me as much as it had, but I had what they call now posttraumatic stress syndrome or what-- whatever it is. And -- for instance, I couldn't-- I couldn't go to a fireworks display because it scared me. I-- I got all nervous and jumpy, so-- and that went on for about a year. And the other thing during that year period was that I used to wake up in the middle of the night screaming. And so it had affected me more than I thought it had. But eventually I was-- I was okay, and so I went on to do the other things that I did. And I had-- we had three children, my wife and I, and -- two sons and a daughter, who are now living-- my older son and my daughter are living in Connecticut, and my younger son is living out on Cape Cod. So, here I am.

sp.speaker: Carolyn Dominiak
sp.p: All right. Is there anything else that you want to-- to add for the record?

sp.speaker: Jasper E. Brady
sp.p: Well, the only other thing we-- we spoke about when I-- when we started out was the fact that we might talk a little bit about my father's service in the Philippines during the first part of the Pacific War. And he was attached to General MacArthur's forces there in the Philippines, and he was a lieutenant colonel when he went overseas, and he was in charge of an infantry battalion. When the Japanese invaded the Philippines, the-- General MacArthur decided to withdraw from the main part of the island out to a peninsula called Bataan. And the-- they set up a defense perimeter on the Bataan Peninsula and fought the Japanese, gradually withdrawing towards the end of the peninsula. And while they were there, they got the-- they got the information from the States that they weren't going to get reinforcements, so they had to fight with the supplies that they had. They were short on food, medicine and ammunition. Their guns wore out after a while because part of that-- the trouble with that being that they were in a tropical area, and that's not exactly good for metal. Any kind of metal. It will rust or wear pretty quickly. And so their guns gave out on them, some of them, although they did try to keep them clean and operating right, but there is a certain amount of wear and tear regardless of what the outfit is and has to be resupplied. But they had no resupply, so they had to do with what they had. They finally fought their way to the end of the Bataan Peninsula, and were so short on food, for instance, that they were down to one third of the rations that they would normally have. Men were ill with malaria, dengue fever, diarrhea, all of that, those sort of things. And some were very weak and couldn't-- couldn't move around very well, but they put up a good fight. And if they'd just had reinforcements, they could have pushed the Japanese right off the island, but they didn't have any.

So, they had-- on April 9th of 1942, the-- General Wainwright, which is-- who was in command of the group at that time -- General MacArthur had pulled back to the island just off the-- off the Bataan Peninsula, which was called Corregidor, and General Wainwright took over and finally surrendered to the Japanese.

So, my father and 75,000 others, Filipino and American troops, were gathered together and marched up the Bataan Peninsula and into the area of Manila and were put into camps. One of them was the Cabanatuan where my father was. And he kept records of all the people that were in his camp and put them in a can and buried them in the ground. And they were dug up and found when the camp was liberated. And they're in possession of-- I think they're in the possession of the War Department now. But anyway, my father, while he was in that camp, was-- he and some of the other officers were put on a ship to be shipped to Japan for slave labor in Japan. But the problem was that the ship was not marked as a prison ship, and it was attacked by our naval air-- aircraft and sunk. And just before it was sunk, they brought all the prisoners up from the hole of the ship to try and wave off the American planes that were attacking it, and-- but it didn't work, and the ship was eventually sunk.

Some of the men got off the ship and swam to shore, but were recaptured. My father died before he could get away, so that's-- he lost his life there on that ship. And that was-- that was in Subic Bay in the Philippines. And so some of those prisoners were-- were liberated from the prison camp when the American forces landed in the southern part of the Philippines and fought their way north, and finally liberated the prisoners after they'd been in the camp for three years.

Some of them made it, and they were brought back to the States and rehabilitated. Some of them stayed in the Service. Others took their discharge. But they formed themselves into a-- into a group, and they called themselves the Battling Bastards of Bataan, and they have their own newspaper and-- which is sent out every couple months. And the survivors of Bataan belong to that group, and they're going to be getting together in May of 19-- or of 2004 at the newly dedicated War Memorial in Washington D.C. at the end of the reflecting pond when that's finished at that time.
So, I'm going down and join them. Oh, that will be fun. And that's about the end of my story, unless you have more questions.

sp.speaker: Carolyn Dominiak
sp.p: Okay.
[END OF INTERVIEW]
